```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
```

voipred.dev evaluates a prediction model in a validation sample in three
steps:

1. `nb()` computes, from the predicted risks of the validation patients, the
   net benefit of the model, of treating everyone and of treating no one, at
   each risk threshold;
2. `plot_dca()` draws the decision curve, or the gain of the model over the
   best default strategy ($\Delta NB$);
3. the value-of-information functions measure how much the uncertainty of a
   finite validation sample matters: `evpi()`, `evsi()`, `p_useful()` and
   `p_best()`, with their plots.

The outcome decides the analysis: a binary outcome (part 1), or a survival or
competing-risks outcome (part 2). Part 3 lists the models voipred can
predict from by itself, when the fitted model is given instead of the risks,
and shows how to use any other model.

This vignette explains each option briefly, with examples. The help pages
give the full details: `?nb`, `?plot_dca`, `?cipcw_control`,
`?predict_risk`, `?nb_priors`, `?evpi`, `?evsi`, `?p_useful`, `?p_best`,
`?plot_evpi`, `?plot_evsi`, `?plot_p_useful` and `?plot_p_best`.

## Installation

voipred.dev and bayespred are installed from GitHub; the other packages used
in this vignette are on CRAN (survival and ggplot2 come with voipred.dev).
plotly (interactive plots) and patchwork (EVPI and EVSI in a panel below the
decision curve) are optional: voipred.dev asks for them only when they are
used. Packages you already have are not installed again; voipred.dev is
always reinstalled, to get its latest version:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
pkgs <- c("remotes", "ranger", "e1071", "riskRegression", "prodlim", "plotly", "patchwork")
new <- pkgs[!vapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(new)) install.packages(new)
if (!requireNamespace("bayespred", quietly = TRUE))
  remotes::install_github("resplab/bayespred")
remotes::install_github("amirfarahmand0/voipred_dev", force = TRUE)   # voipred.dev
```

```{r library}
library(voipred.dev)
library(survival)
```

# Part 1: binary outcome

## Data

The GUSTO-I trial data ships with the package. The outcome is 30-day
mortality (`day30`). We fit the models on a development sample and evaluate
them on a separate validation sample.

```{r data}
set.seed(1)
i   <- sample(nrow(gusto))
dev <- gusto[i[1:5000], ]
val <- gusto[i[5001:10000], ]

mean(val$day30)   # prevalence in the validation sample
```

## Net benefit of one model

`nb()` needs only the predicted risks of the validation patients, given with
`predicted_risk`: one risk per row of `data`. They can come from any model or
software.

```{r glm}
fit_glm <- glm(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
               family = binomial, data = dev)
val$p_glm <- predict(fit_glm, val, type = "response")

res_glm <- nb(predicted_risk = val$p_glm, data = val, outcome = "day30",
              thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01), label = "Logistic")
res_glm
```

The name of the column of `data` that holds the risks works too:
`predicted_risk = "p_glm"` gives the same result.

Instead of the risks, the fitted model can be given, as `model = fit_glm` or
in place of the risks (`nb(fit_glm, val, "day30")`). voipred then predicts
the risks from the model itself, once (part 3). The rest of this guide gives
the models this way.

The result has one row per threshold:

- `NB_model`: net benefit of treating the patients whose predicted risk is at
  or above the threshold;
- `NB_all`: net benefit of treating everyone;
- `NB_none`: net benefit of treating no one (always 0);
- `delta_NB`: $NB_{model} - \max(NB_{all}, NB_{none})$, the gain of the model
  over the best default strategy. The model is useful where it is positive.

## Plots

`plot_dca()` draws the decision curve (`type = "nb"`, the default) or
`delta_NB` (`type = "delta"`):

```{r plot-glm}
plot_dca(res_glm)
plot_dca(res_glm, type = "delta")
```

## Comparing models

Compute `nb()` for each model on the same data and thresholds, then give all
the results to `plot_dca()`:

```{r compare}
fit_rf <- ranger::ranger(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
                         data = dev, probability = TRUE, num.trees = 500, seed = 1)
res_rf <- nb(fit_rf, val, "day30", thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01),
             label = "Random forest")

library(bayespred)
fit_bpm <- bpmfit(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
                  data = dev, prior = log_f(m = 2))
res_bpm <- nb(fit_bpm, val, "day30", thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01),
              label = "Bayesian logistic")

plot_dca(res_glm, res_rf, res_bpm)
plot_dca(res_glm, res_rf, res_bpm, type = "delta")
```

For the bayespred model the risk is the posterior mean of risk.

## Options of `nb()` for a binary outcome

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `predicted_risk` | The predicted risks of the patients in `data`: a vector, one per row (e.g. `val$p_glm`), or the name of the column of `data` that holds them (`"p_glm"`). This is all the validation needs. |
| `model` | Optional, instead of `predicted_risk`: the fitted model. voipred predicts the risks from it, once (part 3). Give either `predicted_risk` or `model`. |
| `data` | The validation sample. With a `model`, it must contain every covariate the model uses. |
| `outcome` | The binary outcome: a column name (`"day30"`), a vector, or a formula (`~ day30`); 0/1, logical, or a two-level factor. |
| `thresholds` | Risk thresholds in [0, 1). Default `seq(0, 0.99, by = 0.01)`. A patient is treated when the risk is at or above the threshold. |
| `weights` | Optional case weights, one per patient (sampling weights, or a bootstrap draw). |
| `predict_function` | Optional, with `model` only: your own function that returns the predicted risks (part 3). |
| `bayesian` | `TRUE` for the Bayesian net benefit (posterior means; see below). Default `FALSE`. |
| `prior` | With `bayesian = TRUE`: `nb_uniform()` (default), `nb_jeffreys()` or your own Beta priors with `nb_beta()`. |
| `label` | Name of the model in printed output and plots. Default: the name of the risks (e.g. `p_glm`) or of the model object. |

See `?nb` for the details of each argument.

**Weights.** An integer weight counts a patient that many times, so
bootstrap draws can be made without copying the data. The weights of an
ordinary bootstrap are the number of times each patient is drawn; those of a
Bayesian bootstrap are Dirichlet(1, ..., 1):

```{r weights}
n <- nrow(val)
z <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20)
set.seed(2)
w_boot <- tabulate(sample(n, replace = TRUE), nbins = n)
w_bb   <- rexp(n); w_bb <- n * w_bb / sum(w_bb)

draws <- rbind(original  = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z)$NB_model,
               bootstrap = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z, weights = w_boot)$NB_model,
               bayesian  = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z, weights = w_bb)$NB_model)
colnames(draws) <- paste("z =", z)
round(draws, 4)
```

**Checks.** voipred stops with a clear message when the risks cannot be
right. Some examples:

```{r checks, error = TRUE}
# a covariate is missing from the validation data
nb(fit_glm, val[, setdiff(names(val), "sysbp")], "day30")

# a forest that only predicts classes (fitted without probability = TRUE)
fit_class <- ranger::ranger(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse,
                            data = dev, num.trees = 100, seed = 1)
nb(fit_class, val, "day30")

# predictions outside [0, 1] are not probabilities
nb(lm(day30 ~ age + Killip, data = dev), val, "day30")

# log-odds given as predicted risks are not probabilities either
nb(predicted_risk = qlogis(val$p_glm), data = val, outcome = "day30")
```

## Options of `plot_dca()`

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `x`, `...` | One or more results of `nb()`. Results drawn together must come from the same data, outcome and thresholds (voipred checks this). |
| `type` | `"nb"`: decision curve with Treat All and Treat None (default). `"delta"`: $\Delta NB$ of each model, with a dashed line at 0. |
| `labels` | Names of the curves, one per result. Default: the `label` of each result. |
| `evpi`, `evsi` | Optional results of `evpi()` and `evsi()`, drawn in a panel below the decision curve (see "Value of information"). The static version needs patchwork. |
| `interactive` | `TRUE` for an interactive plot (needs plotly). Default `FALSE`. |

See `?plot_dca` for details. The plot is a ggplot object, so it can be
changed with `+` or saved with `ggplot2::ggsave()`:

```{r plot-custom, message = FALSE}
p <- plot_dca(res_glm, res_rf, labels = c("Logistic regression", "Forest"))
p + ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.2), ylim = c(-0.005, 0.07))
```

## Interactive plots

Every plot function of voipred takes `interactive = TRUE`, for an
interactive (plotly) version of the same plot: hovering shows the values of
all the curves at that threshold, and clicking a legend entry hides or shows
its curve.

```{r interactive}
plot_dca(res_glm, res_rf, res_bpm, interactive = TRUE)
plot_dca(res_glm, res_rf, res_bpm, type = "delta", interactive = TRUE)
```

## Bayesian net benefit

With `bayesian = TRUE`, `nb()` gives the Bayesian net benefit of bayesDCA
(binary outcome only): the prevalence, the sensitivity and the specificity
of the model at each threshold have conjugate Beta posteriors, and the net
benefit columns are the posterior means. The prior is `nb_uniform()`
(Beta(1, 1), the default), `nb_jeffreys()` (Beta(0.5, 0.5)) or your own
with `nb_beta()`:

```{r bayes-nb}
res_glm_b <- nb(predicted_risk = val$p_glm, data = val, outcome = "day30",
                thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01), bayesian = TRUE,
                label = "Logistic")
head(res_glm_b)

nb_beta(prevalence = c(2, 20))   # a prior for the prevalence, uniform for the rest
```

With 5000 patients the posterior means are close to the ordinary estimates.
The difference is in the uncertainty: the value-of-information functions
below draw from the posterior of a Bayesian result.

## Value of information

The net benefit of a validation sample is an estimate, so the strategy that
looks best may not be the best. The value-of-information functions measure
how much this uncertainty matters (Sadatsafavi et al. 2023, 2025):

- `evpi()`: the expected value of perfect information, the expected loss in
  net benefit from not knowing which strategy (each model, treat all, treat
  none) is best. It is in net benefit units; 0 means the best strategy is
  certain. The relative EVPI is the gain from perfect information relative to
  the gain from using the model now.
- `evsi()`: the expected value of sample information, the expected gain from
  a future validation study of a given size. It is between 0 and EVPI.
- `p_useful()`: the probability that a model is better than both treat all
  and treat none ($\Delta NB > 0$).
- `p_best()`: the probability that each strategy is the best.

They take one or more results of `nb()` for the same data, outcome and
thresholds. The uncertainty is represented by `n_sim` draws (default 1000):
a Bayesian bootstrap (`method = "bayesian"`, the default) or an ordinary
bootstrap (`method = "ordinary"`) of the validation sample, in which the net
benefit of every strategy is recomputed with the same estimator as `nb()`.
The predicted risks stay fixed.

The uncertainty is small with 5000 patients, so here we use a validation
sample of 500, the size of the case study of Sadatsafavi et al. (2023):

```{r voi-data}
small <- val[1:500, ]
z <- seq(0.01, 0.30, by = 0.01)
v_glm <- nb(predicted_risk = small$p_glm, data = small, outcome = "day30",
            thresholds = z, label = "Logistic")
v_rf  <- nb(fit_rf, small, "day30", thresholds = z, label = "Random forest")
```

### EVPI

```{r evpi}
set.seed(10)
e <- evpi(v_glm, v_rf)
head(e)
plot_evpi(e)
plot_evpi(e, type = "relative")
```

`ENB_current` is the expected net benefit of the strategy that is best on
average, and `ENB_perfect` the expected net benefit if the best strategy
were known in each draw. A relative EVPI of 1.2 means that perfect
information would give 20% more net benefit than using the best model now.

### P(useful) and P(best)

```{r p-useful}
set.seed(10)
pu <- p_useful(v_glm, v_rf)
head(pu)
plot_p_useful(pu)

set.seed(10)
pb <- p_best(v_glm, v_rf)
plot_p_best(pb)
```

`evpi()`, `p_useful()` and `p_best()` called with the same seed (and the same
results, `n_sim` and `method`) use the same draws.

### EVSI

`future_n` gives the sizes of the future validation study:

```{r evsi}
set.seed(11)
o <- evsi(v_glm, v_rf, future_n = c(250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000))
head(o)
plot_evsi(o[round(o$threshold, 2) %in% c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2), ])
```

`plot_evsi()` draws EVSI against the future sample size, one curve per
threshold (here four of them), with the EVPI of that threshold as a dashed
line: EVSI approaches EVPI as the future sample grows. Comparing EVSI,
multiplied by the number of patients the decision concerns, with the cost of
the study helps decide whether more validation data are worth collecting.

### The decision curve with EVPI and EVSI

`plot_dca()` draws EVPI and EVSI (one curve per future sample size) in a
panel below the decision curve:

```{r dca-voi, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_dca(v_glm, v_rf, evpi = e, evsi = o)
plot_dca(v_glm, v_rf, evpi = e, evsi = o, interactive = TRUE)
```

### Methods

`method = "ordinary"` uses the ordinary bootstrap instead of the Bayesian
bootstrap. For one model and a binary outcome, `evpi()` also has
`method = "asymptotic"`, a closed form that needs no draws (and the mvtnorm
package):

```{r voi-methods}
set.seed(10)
head(evpi(v_glm, v_rf, method = "ordinary"), 3)
head(evpi(v_glm, method = "asymptotic"), 3)
```

For Bayesian results (`nb(bayesian = TRUE)`), the draws are from the
posterior of the prevalence, sensitivity and specificity instead (as in
bayesDCA), and `method` is not used. Several models are drawn jointly, so
their correlation on the same patients is kept. `evsi()` then uses the
conjugate algorithm of Sadatsafavi et al. (2025):

```{r voi-bayes}
b_glm <- nb(predicted_risk = small$p_glm, data = small, outcome = "day30",
            thresholds = z, bayesian = TRUE, label = "Logistic")
set.seed(12)
e_b <- evpi(b_glm)
set.seed(13)
o_b <- evsi(b_glm, future_n = c(250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000))
plot_dca(b_glm, evpi = e_b, evsi = o_b)
```

The options of the value-of-information functions:

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `x`, `...` | One or more results of `nb()`, for models evaluated on the same data, outcome and thresholds (and horizon, cause and censoring). A named result is labelled with its name. |
| `n_sim` | Number of draws. Default 1000. |
| `method` | `"bayesian"` (Bayesian bootstrap, default) or `"ordinary"` (ordinary bootstrap); `evpi()` also `"asymptotic"`. Not used for Bayesian results. |
| `future_n` | `evsi()` only: the sizes of the future validation sample. |
| `labels` | Optional names of the models, one per result. |

The plot functions `plot_evpi()` (with `type = "evpi"` or `"relative"`),
`plot_evsi()`, `plot_p_useful()` and `plot_p_best()` all take
`interactive = TRUE`. See `?evpi`, `?evsi`, `?p_useful` and `?p_best` for
the details.

# Part 2: survival outcome

## Data

The Rotterdam breast cancer data (from the survival package). The outcome
is death, with time in years; we evaluate the risk of death by 5 years.

```{r surv-data}
rott <- rotterdam
rott$years <- rott$dtime / 365.25
set.seed(1)
j <- sample(nrow(rott))
sdev <- rott[j[1:1500], ]
sval <- rott[j[1501:nrow(rott)], ]
```

## Net benefit of one model

The outcome is given with `Surv()` and the `horizon` is required:

```{r cox}
fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(years, death) ~ age + size + nodes + grade + hormon + chemo,
                 data = sdev)

res_cox <- nb(fit_cox, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5,
              thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01), label = "Cox")
head(res_cox)
```

The columns are the same as for a binary outcome; the event is "death by 5
years". The prevalence is the estimated risk of death by 5 years. Predicted
risks given with `predicted_risk` must be the risks of the event by the
horizon (for competing risks, of the cause by the horizon).

## Plots

The same `plot_dca()` as for a binary outcome: the decision curve and
`delta_NB`.

```{r cox-plot}
plot_dca(res_cox)
plot_dca(res_cox, type = "delta")
```

## Comparing models

```{r surv-plot}
fit_aft <- survreg(Surv(years, death) ~ age + size + nodes, data = sdev,
                   dist = "weibull")
res_aft <- nb(fit_aft, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5,
              thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01), label = "Weibull AFT")

plot_dca(res_cox, res_aft)
plot_dca(res_cox, res_aft, type = "delta")
```

## Options of `nb()` for a survival outcome

All the options of part 1 apply. In addition:

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `outcome` | `~ Surv(time, status)`, with status 1 = event and 0 = censored. For competing risks, status is a factor whose first level is censoring (see below). |
| `horizon` | The time by which the risk is predicted and the event counted (required), in the units of the survival times. |
| `censoring` | How censoring is handled: `"km"` (default) or `"cipcw"` (see below). |
| `cipcw` | With `censoring = "cipcw"`: the censoring model or weights, made with `cipcw_control()`. |
| `cause` | Competing risks only: the event type of interest (default: the first event level). |

See `?nb` for the details of each argument.

**Censoring: `"km"`.** The risk among the treated patients is a
Kaplan-Meier estimate (Aalen-Johansen for competing risks), as in dcurves.
It assumes that censoring is independent of the outcome. At a threshold where
none of the treated patients is followed up to the horizon, the net benefit
cannot be estimated: it is `NA`, with a warning.

**Censoring: `"cipcw"`.** Conditional inverse probability of censoring
weighting allows censoring to depend on covariates. Fit a model to the
censoring times of the validation data, with censoring as the event
(`Surv(time, status == 0)`), and give it with `cipcw_control()`. The
censoring model can be any of the survival models voipred supports as
prediction models (part 3), e.g. a Cox model, a parametric model or a
random survival forest; for any other model, give its `predict_function` in
`cipcw_control()`, or give the weights directly.

```{r cipcw}
cens <- coxph(Surv(years, death == 0) ~ age + nodes + grade, data = sval)

res_cipcw <- nb(fit_cox, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5,
                thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01),
                censoring = "cipcw", cipcw = cipcw_control(model = cens),
                label = "Cox")
plot_dca(res_cipcw)
plot_dca(res_cipcw, type = "delta")
```

Results with different censoring methods are different estimates, so
`plot_dca()` does not draw them together.

The options of `cipcw_control()`:

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `model` | A survival model fitted to the censoring times of the validation data: any of the survival models voipred supports (part 3). |
| `predict_function` | Optional: your own function giving the probability of remaining uncensored, for a censoring model voipred cannot predict from. |
| `refit_function` | Optional: your own function that refits the censoring model with case weights, used by the value-of-information functions (see below). |
| `weight_event`, `weight_horizon` | Instead of a model: the censoring weights themselves, e.g. from a cross-fitted flexible model. |
| `min_prob` | Optional truncation of small censoring probabilities (large weights). Off by default. |
| `ties` | `"left"` (default) or `"right"`: whether a censoring at exactly a patient's own time counts. |

See `?cipcw_control` for the details.

## Competing risks

With competing risks, the status is a factor whose first level is censoring
and whose other levels are the event types. Here the events are recurrence and
death, whichever comes first, and the model is a cause-specific Cox model:

```{r competing}
crdat <- function(d) {
  d$cr_time   <- ifelse(d$recur == 1, d$rtime, d$dtime) / 365.25
  d$cr_code   <- ifelse(d$recur == 1, 1, ifelse(d$death == 1, 2, 0))
  d$cr_status <- factor(d$cr_code, 0:2, c("censored", "recurrence", "death"))
  d
}
sdev <- crdat(sdev)
sval <- crdat(sval)

fit_csc <- riskRegression::CSC(prodlim::Hist(cr_time, cr_code) ~ age + size + nodes + grade,
                               data = sdev)
res_csc <- nb(fit_csc, sval, ~ Surv(cr_time, cr_status), horizon = 5,
              cause = "recurrence", thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01),
              label = "Cause-specific Cox")
head(res_csc)
plot_dca(res_csc)
plot_dca(res_csc, type = "delta")
```

The net benefit is for "recurrence by 5 years": a patient who died first
counts as not having the event.

cIPCW works with competing risks in the same way. Only true censoring is
censoring: the censoring model is fitted with the censored patients as the
events (`cr_status == "censored"`), and patients with a competing event are
not censored. voipred stops if the censoring model was fitted to one of the
causes instead.

```{r competing-cipcw}
cens_cr <- coxph(Surv(cr_time, cr_status == "censored") ~ age + nodes + grade,
                 data = sval)

res_csc_cipcw <- nb(fit_csc, sval, ~ Surv(cr_time, cr_status), horizon = 5,
                    cause = "recurrence", thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01),
                    censoring = "cipcw", cipcw = cipcw_control(model = cens_cr),
                    label = "Cause-specific Cox")
plot_dca(res_csc_cipcw)
plot_dca(res_csc_cipcw, type = "delta")
```

## Value of information

The value-of-information functions work for survival and competing-risks
outcomes in the same way, with the same estimator as `nb()` (Kaplan-Meier,
Aalen-Johansen or cIPCW) in every draw:

```{r surv-voi, fig.height = 6.5}
set.seed(20)
e_s <- evpi(res_cox, res_aft)
set.seed(21)
o_s <- evsi(res_cox, res_aft, future_n = c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000))
plot_dca(res_cox, res_aft, evpi = e_s, evsi = o_s)

set.seed(22)
plot_p_best(p_best(res_csc))
```

With `censoring = "cipcw"`, the censoring model is refitted in every draw,
so the uncertainty of the censoring weights is included. This is automatic
for `coxph`, `survreg`, `rms::cph`, `rms::psm`, `flexsurvreg` and `prodlim`
censoring models:

```{r surv-voi-cipcw}
set.seed(23)
e_c <- evpi(res_cipcw, n_sim = 500)
e_c[seq(11, 51, by = 10), ]   # thresholds 0.1, 0.2, ..., 0.5
```

For any other censoring model, give `refit_function` in `cipcw_control()`: a
`function(data, weights)` that returns the censoring model fitted to `data`
with case weights `weights`. (With `method = "ordinary"`, a model that does
not take case weights is refitted to the resampled patients instead.)
Censoring weights given directly cannot be refitted, so they can be used in
`nb()` but not in the value-of-information functions.

```{r surv-voi-refit}
cipcw_rf <- cipcw_control(
  model = cens,
  refit_function = function(data, weights)
    coxph(Surv(years, death == 0) ~ age + nodes + grade, data = data, weights = weights))
res_cipcw2 <- nb(fit_cox, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5,
                 thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01),
                 censoring = "cipcw", cipcw = cipcw_rf, label = "Cox")
set.seed(23)
evpi(res_cipcw2, n_sim = 500)[seq(11, 51, by = 10), ]
```

Here the refit is the same as voipred's own refit of a `coxph` model, so the
results are the same.

# Part 3: which models work

## Models voipred supports

When the fitted model is given instead of the predicted risks, voipred
predicts the risks from it, once: the probability of the event (binary), of
the event by the horizon (survival), or of the cause by the horizon
(competing risks). For the following models this works without anything
else, and each is tested against the model's own predictions:

- **Binary:** `glm` (logit, probit, cloglog), `logistf`, `mgcv::gam`,
  `earth`, `rpart`, `partykit::ctree`, `randomForest`, `ranger`
  (`probability = TRUE`), `gbm`, `xgboost`, `lightgbm`, `catboost`,
  `glmnet`, `cv.glmnet`, `e1071::svm` (`probability = TRUE`),
  `e1071::naiveBayes`, `naivebayes`, `nnet`, `MASS::lda`, `MASS::qda`,
  `kknn`, and **bayespred** (`bpmfit`, `bpm`).
- **Survival:** `coxph`, `rms::cph`, `survreg`, `rms::psm`, `flexsurvreg`,
  `flexsurvspline`, `rstpm2::stpm2`, `mgcv::gam` (`cox.ph()`), `ranger`,
  `randomForestSRC`, `aorsf`, `partykit::ctree`, `prodlim`, and
  **bayespred.dev** Bayesian Cox and parametric survival models.
- **Competing risks:** `riskRegression::CSC`, `riskRegression::FGR`,
  `cmprsk::crr`, competing-risks `randomForestSRC`, and survival's multi-state
  `coxph`.
- **Censoring models (cIPCW):** the same survival models as above, fitted to
  the censoring times. voipred gets from them the probability of remaining
  uncensored, for survival and competing-risks outcomes alike.

"Supported" means only that voipred knows how to get predicted probabilities
from the fitted model. It says nothing about whether the model is a good
one, which is what the net benefit is for. Any other model whose `predict()`
returns probabilities in the usual way, or that has a
`riskRegression::predictRisk()` method, works too. See `?predict_risk` for how
the risks are obtained.

## Any other model: `predict_function`

For a model voipred cannot predict from, either compute the risks yourself
and give them with `predicted_risk`, or give the model with
`predict_function`: a function
of `(model, newdata, horizon, cause)` that returns one predicted risk per row
of `newdata`. voipred calls it once, with `newdata = data`. It is optional:
voipred uses its own route by default, and `predict_function` only when you
give it, in which case it always replaces voipred's own route.

A binary example (an SVM, which voipred also handles by itself):

```{r pf-binary}
fit_svm <- e1071::svm(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse, data = dev,
                      probability = TRUE)
vars <- c("age", "Killip", "sysbp", "pulse")
nb(fit_svm, val, "day30", thresholds = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2),
   predict_function = function(model, newdata, ...) {
     pr <- predict(model, newdata[, vars], probability = TRUE)
     attr(pr, "probabilities")[, "1"]
   })
```

A survival example: the function receives the `horizon` and returns the risk
of the event by then (here from `survfit()`, for illustration):

```{r pf-survival}
nb(fit_cox, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5, thresholds = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3),
   predict_function = function(model, newdata, horizon, ...) {
     sf <- survfit(model, newdata = newdata)
     1 - as.vector(summary(sf, times = horizon)$surv)
   })
```

The function's output is checked like any other: it must be one probability
per patient, in [0, 1], and not only 0s and 1s. A censoring model can be
given its own `predict_function` in the same way, in `cipcw_control()`.
